title: ITC Hotels Plants Its Flag in Kerala's Backwaters with ₹205-Crore Kumarakom Acquisition
excerpt: The debt-free deal for Zuri Kumarakom Resort & Spa gives ITC its first owned property in Kerala — and NRI travellers a luxury option on one of India's most coveted coastlines.
body:
ITC Hotels has agreed to acquire The Zuri Kumarakom Kerala Resort & Spa for ₹205 crore, a deal that gives India's largest domestic luxury hospitality chain its first owned property in a state that receives over a million foreign tourists a year — a significant share of them from the Indian diaspora.

The acquisition, approved by ITC Hotels' board this week, is a 100% stake purchase of Zuri Hotels & Resorts Pvt Ltd. It is a debt-free transaction: ITC is buying the company outright, along with its crown jewel — an 18-acre waterfront resort nestled along the famed Vembanad Lake backwaters, featuring 72 rooms across 38 private villas, a five-acre man-made lagoon, and an Ayurvedic wellness centre.

## Why Kerala, Why Now

Kerala has long punched above its weight in Indian tourism. The state's "God's Own Country" branding, built on backwaters, Ayurveda, and a literate, English-speaking population, made it one of the first Indian destinations that NRIs felt comfortable recommending to non-Indian friends. But Kerala's luxury hotel stock has not kept pace with demand. Much of the high-end inventory remains boutique-scale or independently managed, lacking the consistency and loyalty-programme infrastructure that well-travelled diaspora visitors expect.

ITC's entry addresses that gap directly. The company plans phased renovations of the Kumarakom property, rebranding it under the ITC Hotels umbrella and integrating it with the chain's "Rooted in the Soil" culinary philosophy — which emphasises regional ingredients, local cooking traditions, and sustainable sourcing. For a resort in Kumarakom, that means fresh karimeen (pearl spot fish), appam and stew, and toddy-tapped coconut preparations elevated to fine-dining standards.

## The Numbers Behind the Move

The deal makes financial sense on its own terms. ITC Hotels reported record revenue of ₹4,139 crore for FY26, up 16% year-on-year, with net profit surging 39% to ₹888 crore. The company declared its first-ever dividend of ₹1 per share. Against that backdrop, ₹205 crore for a waterfront Kerala resort looks like a rounding error — and management has told analysts it expects to triple the property's revenue post-renovation.

The acquisition also fits a broader industry pattern. India's luxury hospitality sector is consolidating as branded chains absorb independent resorts that thrived pre-pandemic but struggled with rising operational costs and the pressure to invest in technology, sustainability certifications, and global distribution. Zuri, which had built a loyal following for its location and Ayurvedic spa, simply needed deeper pockets to compete at the next level.

## What NRI Travellers Should Know

For diaspora Indians planning their next trip to Kerala — whether a family reunion, a destination wedding, or a post-retirement roots journey — the ITC rebrand changes the calculus in practical ways.

First, loyalty points. ITC Hotels' membership programme, integrated with global platforms, means that points accumulated at ITC Maurya in Delhi or ITC Grand Chola in Chennai will soon be redeemable in Kumarakom. For NRIs who already default to ITC properties during India visits, this adds a leisure destination to what was primarily a business-travel portfolio.

Second, Ayurvedic wellness. Zuri's existing spa programme, already popular with international guests, will be expanded under ITC's "Kaya Kalp" wellness brand — a standardised but culturally rooted spa concept that has won awards at properties across India. For health-conscious NRIs interested in authentic Ayurvedic treatments rather than hotel-spa approximations, this could be a draw.

Third, weddings and celebrations. Kumarakom's backwater setting has made it one of South India's most photographed wedding venues. ITC's event-management infrastructure — honed at properties that regularly host 500-guest celebrations — should make the logistics smoother and the options more elaborate.

## A Bet on Experiential India

ITC's Kumarakom acquisition is ultimately a bet on a specific kind of Indian tourism: experiential, wellness-oriented, and culturally immersive. It is the opposite of the beach-resort model that dominates Goa or the temple-circuit approach of Rajasthan. Kerala sells transformation — slow mornings on houseboats, oil-drip Ayurvedic therapies, spice-garden walks that end in cooking lessons.

For the Indian diaspora, this kind of travel is increasingly the point. The days when NRIs visited India purely for family obligations are fading; what is replacing them is a deliberate, curated engagement with the country's landscapes and traditions. ITC, with its deep pockets and appetite for luxury, appears to be positioning itself as the default brand for that journey.
